input.explanation:
What the fault is: `typical_spend_per_item` - the account-page figure that the rollout flag switches on - finds the middle of a shopper's history by removing the cheapest remaining price over and over. Each removal scans everything that is left, so the work is quadratic in the number of purchases: a shopper with a long history costs the page one whole walk of that history per purchase. Every page is still correct, which is why nothing shows in the error rate; the only thing that moves is how long a render takes.

Why the flag exposed it: with the flag off, the page serves the lifetime or monthly average and never enters this function. Turning `monthly-spend-feature` on routes requests into it, and at 16:06, with every request on the new figure, p99 went from ~200ms to 1702ms. The toggle is not the fault - the fault is code whose cost grows with the square of a shopper's history sitting on the most-visited page in the shop. Rolling the flag back hid it and left it there.

The fix: order the prices once and read the middle off. Same figure for every history - same lower-of-two-middles behaviour on an even-length history, same handling of repeated prices (the prices are sorted as a list, so a repeated price still occupies one slot per purchase) - at n log n instead of n². The empty history still raises `ValueError`, exactly as `min()` on an empty sequence did, so the request boundary in `io_shop.account_page` turns it into the same failed page it did before; nothing downstream sees a new exception type.

The test: `test_the_middle_is_found_without_rescanning_the_history_for_every_purchase` counts price comparisons using an `int` subclass and asserts the work stays within a small multiple of the history length. Against the code as it stands, a 2,000-purchase history costs roughly 1.5 million comparisons and the test fails; against the fix it costs about 22,000 and passes. It is a bound on work done rather than on the answer, because the old code returns the right answer too - slowly. A correctness assertion on the same large history is included so the cheap path is still pinned to the right figure.</explanation>

from io_shop.accounts import Account


def typical_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
    """The middle price in this shopper's history.

    The prices are put in order once and the middle one is read off. On an
    even-length history that lands on the lower of the two middles, which is
    the one a shopper reading "your typical purchase" can point at - a figure
    interpolated between two prices is one nobody paid.

    of a shopper's history on the most-visited page in the shop. Sorting is the
    same answer - a repeated price occupies one slot per purchase either way -
    at a cost that grows with the history rather than with its square.

    A history with nothing in it has no middle, and says so rather than
    guessing, exactly as the empty `min()` did before it. The request boundary
    turns that into a failed page - see `io_shop.account_page`.
    """
    prices = sorted(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases)

    if not prices:
        raise ValueError("a history with no purchases has no middle price")

    return prices[(len(prices) - 1) // 2]

from io_shop.accounts import Account, Purchase
from io_shop.typical_spend import typical_spend_per_item

    # whole point of showing the middle rather than the average is that a

def test_repeated_prices_do_not_lose_the_middle() -> None:

    assert typical_spend_per_item(a_history_of_coffees_and_a_laptop) == 300


class _CountedPrice(int):
    """An amount in pence that remembers being compared with another.

    An int, so the figure that comes back out of the module is the figure a

    how_many = 2_000

"""What this shopper's middle purchase cost.

The newest thing on the account page, and the one still behind a rollout. An
average is dragged around by a single expensive buy - one laptop among twenty
coffees averages to a figure describing neither - so the page offers the middle
of the history instead: the price as many purchases sit below as above.

The figure it produces is right for every history the shop has, and it costs
one ordering of that history to produce - not one walk of the history per
purchase in it, which is what it used to cost and what put the account page's
p99 into the seconds the first time the rollout reached every request.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from io_shop.accounts import Account


def typical_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
    """The middle price in this shopper's history.

    The prices are put in order once and the middle one is read off. On an
    even-length history that lands on the lower of the two middles, which is
    the one a shopper reading "your typical purchase" can point at - a figure
    interpolated between two prices is one nobody paid.

    Ordered once rather than found by taking the cheapest that is left, over
    and over. That selection was correct and quadratic: every removal scanned
    everything still remaining, so the cost of this figure grew with the square
    of a shopper's history on the most-visited page in the shop. Sorting is the
    same answer - a repeated price occupies one slot per purchase either way -
    at a cost that grows with the history rather than with its square.

    A history with nothing in it has no middle, and says so rather than
    guessing, exactly as the empty `min()` did before it. The request boundary
    turns that into a failed page - see `io_shop.account_page`.
    """
    prices = sorted(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases)

    if not prices:
        raise ValueError("a history with no purchases has no middle price")

    return prices[(len(prices) - 1) // 2]

        total_cents=sum(prices),
        total_this_month_cents=0,
    )


def test_the_middle_price_of_an_odd_history_is_the_one_in_the_middle() -> None:

def test_repeated_prices_do_not_lose_the_middle() -> None:

    # the same thing five times has a middle, and it is that thing.
